newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico seethes as countryman executed in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Mexico seethes as countryman executed in U.S.

text.p: Mexicans reacted with anger on Wednesday after one of their countrymen was put to death in a Texas jail, and grief-stricken family members condemned his executioners as murderers.

Tears, cries of outrage and hysteria met news of the death of Irineo Tristan Montoya, 30, who shortly after 6 pm CDT (2300 GMT) became the fourth Mexican to be executed in the United States this century.
He was injected at Huntsville state prison in Texas with a dose of lethal chemicals.

Some 500 protestors, including family members, who had blocked the border bridge linking Matamoros and Brownsville, Texas in a vain attempt to stop the execution, reacted in fury after they heard Tristan had been pronounced dead.
"What bastards, what a pack of murderers," an aunt of Tristan, who gave her name only as Amalia, cried out.
"They are butchers," said Jose Luis Tristan, another member of the dead man's family.
Tristan's execution has stirred heated passions across Mexico, where the death sentence for civilians is banned.

The blow was compounded by the fact Tristan died at the hands of the U.S. justice system, which many here believe is biased against the millions of Mexicans who, like Tristan, seek work in the United States.
In his last days, Tristan's battle for life became the talk of Mexico's streets and the main item in the news.

On Mexico's main television news programme, anchor Jacobo Zabludovsky of the Televisa network wore a black tie in mourning, and just prior to the death the station's reporter in Huntsville could be heard choking back tears as he described Tristan's final hours.
Tristan was convicted for the 1985 murder of John Kilheffer, who was stabbed more than 22 times and whose body was dumped in a grapefruit grove near the Rio Grande
Televisa, whose widely-watched commentators have lambasted the execution, described Tristan's fate as "administrative assassination."

Radio Red reported that Mexico's Catholic Church sent a letter of protest to Texas Gov. George Bush, who refused a request to delay the execution despite an impassioned last-minute plea from Tristan's mother, who herself is dying of lung cancer.

The Mexican Foreign Ministry in a statement late on Wednesday said it deeply regretted that the death penalty had been carried out, despite repeated attempts to save Tristan's life. It said it was a "cruel and inhuman" form of punishment.
But Mexico's consul-general in Houston, Manuel Perez Cardenas, predicted ties between the two countries would not be strained by the execution.

Callers flooded national radio stations criticising the act, demanding that the executioners be brought to account, and blaming their own government for not providing enough work in Mexico to stop countrymen emigrating north.
One caller urged Mexicans to stop eating American hamburgers in protest at their countryman's death.
